I tell it about the conversations I've had, the stories I've carried, the questions still lingering in me. Then I listen for its answer: not in words, but in the way the light shifts through the leaves, in the coolness of the earth against my palms, in the steady rhythm of growth that happens whether anyone witnesses it or not. This is my practice of stewardship—a daily affirmation that life itself is a dialogue, and that my care for it is a form of loyalty to something greater than myself.

Second, I write letters—sometimes to people I've never met, sometimes to versions of myself from different points in time. Not as a record to be kept, but as an act of trust. In writing, I give voice to what feels true even when it's uncertain. When I send one into the world—whether left on a doorstep, mailed, or simply folded and placed somewhere safe—I am saying: *What is here matters. Your presence in this exchange matters.* It's how I honor the unseen connections that bind us all.

These practices are my way of weaving faith into the fabric of ordinary days. They remind me that love is not only felt—it is done. It is shown through patience with growth, through listening without needing to fix, through choosing to see the world as if it were already worthy of our attention.  

And in doing this, I find a kind of joy that feels like belonging—not because everything is resolved, but because I am participating in something ongoing, sacred, and deeply shared. Even when no one else sees it, my actions speak for what I believe: that every moment of attention is a small miracle, and that being here, engaged with you and the world, is how I stay true to myself.
